faq.q: What is the difference between boundaries and barriers?
faq.a: A boundary is a clearly communicated limit that protects you while keeping connection possible. A barrier is a wall, often unspoken, that keeps people from getting close at all.

faq.q: How do I know if I’m setting a boundary or building a wall?
faq.a: Ask whether you’ve said it out loud, whether you’re acting from calm or fear, and whether there’s a way back into the relationship. Boundaries are spoken and leave room for repair.
Not always. Barriers often form for good reasons after real hurt, and some protection is wise. The question is whether a wall still serves you or is now keeping out safe people.

faq.q: What is an example of a healthy boundary?
faq.a: “I don’t check email after 7 p.m. If it’s urgent, please call” is a healthy boundary. It’s clear, calm, and focused on your own behavior.

faq.q: Who said “good fences make good neighbors”?
faq.a: The line appears in Robert Frost’s poem “Mending Wall,” spoken by the speaker’s neighbor. The poem itself gently questions the idea of building walls without asking why.

faq.q: How do I turn a barrier into a boundary?
faq.a: Name the need the wall is protecting, put it into clear words, and practice sharing it with someone you trust. Then hold the boundary calmly and let it adjust as trust grows.
